stem:
Two series of annual sales figures are summarised below:

Series P: Mean = 25 lakhs, Standard Deviation = 5 lakhs
Series Q: Mean = 20 lakhs, Standard Deviation = 6 lakhs

Which series shows GREATER relative variability and what is its coefficient of variation?

options.text: Both series have equal relative variability

per_option_rationale.rationale: CV_P = (5/25)*100 = 20%. CV_Q = (6/20)*100 = 30%. Series Q has higher CV so it shows greater relative variability.

Student compares the SD values (5 vs 6) and concludes P is less variable, then incorrectly selects P as having greater variation due to confusing the question direction; or uses mean as the comparator since P has a higher mean.
Student computes CV_Q = (SD_Q / mean_P)*100 = (6/25)*100 = 24%, mixing up the denominators of the two series.
Student confuses CV with an invariant property and incorrectly believes that since the two SDs are close (5 and 6) the relative variation must be similar.

explanation: Coefficient of variation = (SD / mean) * 100. It measures relative dispersion and is the correct tool for comparing variability across series with different means.

explanation_sections.punchline: The setup decision is using CV (not raw SD) when comparing variability across series with different means.
explanation_sections.approach: Step 1: Identify the right measure: different means require CV for valid comparison. Step 2: CV_P = (5/25)*100 = 20%. Step 3: CV_Q = (6/20)*100 = 30%. Step 4: 30% > 20%, so Series Q has greater relative variability.
explanation_sections.lesson: Raw SD is only comparable when the two means are equal; use CV for relative comparisons across different scales.
explanation_sections.timing: About 45 seconds. Two divisions and two comparisons. The trap is to choose Q because its SD is larger (6 > 5), which happens to be correct here but for the wrong reason.
